lines.say: Your qubit, a quantum bit, reads zero every time you check it. How can you make it read one?
Picture the qubit as an arrow. Up means zero, and down means one.
To change it, we use a gate, which turns the arrow without stretching it.
Our first gate is called X, and it's like flipping a pancake.
Flip the pan, and the pancake's top ends up on the bottom.
Flip it again, and you're back where you started.
X does the same to our arrow, a half turn around a line running left to right.
The arrow pointing up at zero lands pointing down at one.
It's the not gate of ordinary computers, swapping zero and one every time, with no chance involved.
Do X twice, and two half turns make a full turn, so you're back home.
Here the pancake falls short. It's always one side up, but our arrow can point in between.
Say it leans toward the top, so it reads zero eight times out of ten.
After the same half turn, it leans low and reads one eight times out of ten.
X has swapped how much zero and how much one the arrow holds.
X doesn't read the qubit and then flip it. It turns the whole arrow, lean and all.
Up is written ket zero, and down is ket one, so X turns ket zero into ket one and ket one into ket zero.
So remember, gates turn the arrow, and X is the half turn that swaps zero and one.
